Chapter 9: The Politics of Fear and the Challenge of Moving Forward
Even as more and more evidence stacked up in favor of real change, the politics of fear still had a tight grip on the conversation.
Think about election season—candidates love to promise crackdowns and harsher penalties, tapping right into our deepest anxieties about safety and order.
The news? It tends to zero in on the most sensational stories, which just reinforces this idea that drugs and crime always go hand in hand.
In one city, a heart-breaking overdose set off a wave of calls for a return to zero-tolerance policies.
Parents, desperate for answers, demanded action. And politicians, wanting to look tough, rushed new laws through with barely any debate.
It’s a pattern we’ve seen over and over: more arrests, more prisons, and more families left struggling to pick up the pieces.
But here’s where things start to shift.
Underneath all that, something new was bubbling up. More police officers, judges, and even former prosecutors started speaking out against the war on drugs.
They’d seen the damage with their own eyes—lives wasted, families broken, and entire communities left behind. Some were willing to risk their own careers to stand up for what they believed in, joining forces with activists and people in recovery to push for a different approach.
Now, the fight was far from finished.
In lots of places, efforts to reform stalled out, or even got rolled back. But here’s the thing—the conversation had changed.
People couldn’t just ignore the evidence anymore, or pretend that punishment, on its own, could fix everything.
The real challenge now? Building on the progress that’s already been made, resisting the old knee-jerk reactions, and keeping our eyes on what actually works.
